title: PLATO: Pointer Learner for Agent and Task Openness

images.desc:
4 Methodology


PLATO is a CTDE method for multi-agent systems with TO and AO, as shown in Figure 1. PLATO’s core novelty is reformulating action selection from fixed-index classification to content-based pointing: each agent forms a context vector (query) and selects among the currently available tasks by matching this query against task feature vectors (keys). The policy output size is determined by the current task set, so tasks and agents can appear or disappear without retraining or architectural changes, keeping the policy well-defined as openness changes the environment.


Figure 1: PLATO architecture for OASYS. It uses a pointer actor approach and CTDE training. 



4.1 Pointer Actor


The pointer actor is the decentralized policy used at execution time. It supports TO by producing a policy whose support matches the currently available tasks, and supports AO by conditioning decisions on a permutation-invariant summary of the current team. The actor (1) deterministically factors oito_{i}^{t} into an agent-feature matrix and a task-feature matrix, (2) encodes the current agent set into a fixed-dimensional query, (3) encodes each available task into a key, and (4) applies additive cross-attention to obtain a categorical distribution over the available task-actions.




4.2 Observation Factorization


In TaAgO-MG, the observation of the ithi^{\text{th}} agent at time tt, oito_{i}^{t}, is its local view of the global state, Statet\mathrm{State}^{t}, restricted to the current agent set NtN^{t} and task set XtX^{t} that are visible or relevant to agent ii.
The preprocessor factors oio_{i} into an agent-feature matrix oNt∈ℝ|Nt|×fNo_{N}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|N^{t}|\times f_{N}} and a task-feature matrix oXt∈ℝ|Xt|×fXo_{X}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|X^{t}|\times f_{X}}. In these feature matrices, rows correspond to ii’s observation of tasks and other agents, similar to node factorization for MOHITO’s critic graph (Anil et al., 2025).

Preprocessor.
Each agent ii receives a local observation oit∈Oto_{i}^{t}\in O^{t} covering the agents and tasks relevant to ii at time tt. A deterministic preprocessor factors this into an agent-feature matrix and a task-feature matrix:




oNt∈ℝ|Nt|×fN,oXt∈ℝ|Xt|×fX.o^{t}_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{|N^{t}|\times f_{N}},\quad o^{t}_{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{|X^{t}|\times f_{X}}.



Encoder.
This step constructs one query from the agent set and a variable-sized set of keys from the task set. We use MLP encoders since the actor makes a single decision per timestep from fully observable features; sequential decoding is not required.
We address AO by aggregating four statistics (i.e., mean, variance, minimum, and maximum) over agents in oNto^{t}_{N} to produce a fixed-length vector dtd^{t} (Alg. 1, line 10) and then encoding it as qt=MLPs​(dt)q^{t}=\mathrm{MLP}_{s}(d^{t}) (Alg. 1, line 11).
In Lemma 1, we show the encoder is permutation invariant to agent order (proof in Appendix A.1).
We use multiple statistics to reduce aliasing, where different agent sets could otherwise produce identical representations. We address TO through attention. We construct |Xt|+1|X^{t}|+1 keys KtK^{t} from oXto^{t}_{X} (Alg. 1, line 12) in the task encoder: one key kxt=MLPx​(oxt)k_{x}^{t}=\mathrm{MLP}_{x}(o_{x}^{t}) per task, plus a no-op key. We assume one action per task with a persistent no-op, so ait={no-op}∪{ax∣x∈Xt}a_{i}^{t}=\{\textsc{no-op}\}\cup\{a_{x}\mid x\in X^{t}\}.



Lemma 1 (Encoder Permutation Invariance).


Each team statistic is permutation invariant, M​L​PsMLP_{s} operates on the aggregate, and M​L​PxMLP_{x} operates on task observations independently. Therefore, the agent and task encodings are permutation invariant.



Pointer Decoder.


The Pointer Decoder is a one-step variant of a pointer network (Vinyals et al., 2015) that maps the query and keys to a stochastic policy over currently available task-actions. We use one-step, additive attention (Bahdanau et al., 2014) to decode (qt,kxt)(q^{t},k_{x}^{t}) to uxtu_{x}^{t}, a scalar attention score (Alg. 1, line 13), in which, 𝐖K\mathbf{W}_{K} and 𝐖q\mathbf{W}_{q} are learnable projection matrices, and
𝐯\mathbf{v} is a learnable vector projecting the compatibility space to a scalar score. We then normalize over all attention scores using SOFTMAX to obtain the policy (Alg. 1, line 14).





4.3 GNN Critic


The critic is centralized during training and estimates Vϕ​(st)V_{\phi}(s^{t}) under CTDE. It represents the open global state as a bipartite agent–task graph whose node sets vary with |Nt||N^{t}| and |Xt||X^{t}|. Agent and task features are embedded into a shared latent space, message passing propagates relational information across agent–task edges, and pooling yields a fixed-size graph summary that is mapped to a scalar value. This avoids fixed-size concatenation and supports variable numbers of agents and tasks.


𝒢t=⟨𝒳t,𝒩t,ℰt⟩\mathcal{G}^{t}=\langle\mathcal{X}^{t},\mathcal{N}^{t},\mathcal{E}^{t}\rangle
encodes the state, Statet\text{State}^{t}, at time tt, where
(1) 𝒳t∈ℝ|Xt|×fX\mathcal{X}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|X^{t}|\times f_{X}} are task nodes and contain fXf_{X} many features, describing each task at time tt; (2) 𝒩t∈ℝ|Nt|×fN\mathcal{N}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|N^{t}|\times f_{N}} are agent nodes and contain fNf_{N} many features, describing each agent at time tt; and (3)
ℰt\mathcal{E}^{t} includes undirected edges between all agent-task pairs which have an action, {⟨n,x⟩|n∈𝒩t​ and ​x∈𝒳t}\{\langle n,x\rangle|n\in\mathcal{N}^{t}\text{ and }x\in\mathcal{X}^{t}\}.


We build a critic network using a GCN (Kipf and Welling, 2016) to propagate information between agent and task nodes by message passing. First, we use MLP encoders to map 𝒩t\mathcal{N}^{t} and 𝒳t\mathcal{X}^{t} into a shared latent space and concatenate them to form 𝐡0t\mathbf{h}_{0}^{t} (Alg. 1, line 18), where 𝐡0t\mathbf{h}_{0}^{t} is the embedding of all nodes in 𝒢t\mathcal{G}^{t} and fhf_{h} is the hidden dimension. We then perform message passing (Alg. 1, line 19) with a skip connection (He et al., 2016) that adds 𝐡0t\mathbf{h}_{0}^{t} to the final layer output before pooling, preserving individual node features that would otherwise be smoothed out by message passing. We use two layers to allow information to propagate between agents and tasks through the bipartite graph.
Finally, we map the node embeddings to a scalar value by mean pooling over nodes followed by an MLPv\mathrm{MLP}_{v} value head (Alg. 1, lines 20–21). We outline in Theorem 1 and show in Appendix A.2 that the actor and critic are well defined functions over the open task and agent spaces.



Theorem 1 (PLATO is well defined).


The actor and critic are permutation invariant, as shown in Lemma 1 and Appendix A.2. The MLPs act on observations independently or on aggregates. The pointer decoder and critic GCNs are defined over a single unbounded dimension. Therefore, the actor and critic are well defined functions over the countably infinite open agent–task space.





4.4 Training


We train PLATO under CTDE using MAPPO ((Yu et al., 2022; Schulman et al., 2017)) with a centralized critic and a single shared policy, while at execution time only the decentralized pointer actor is used. The actor is optimized with the PPO clipped objective ((Schulman et al., 2017)). The critic uses the standard PPO clipped value regression loss, and we compute advantages with generalized advantage estimation (GAE) (Schulman et al., 2015) (Alg. 1, line 6). All actor (θ={M​L​PS,M​L​PX,𝐖K,𝐖q}\theta=\{MLP_{S},MLP_{X},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{q}\}) and critic (ϕ={M​L​P𝒳,M​L​P𝒩,M​L​Pv,GCNs}\phi=\{MLP_{\mathcal{X}},MLP_{\mathcal{N}},MLP_{v},\text{GCNs}\}) components are standard differentiable modules optimized jointly. The per-timestep training cost holds all neural network dimensions constant and scales only with the number of active agents |Nt||N^{t}| and active tasks |Xt||X^{t}|, as formalized in Theorem 2 (proof details in Appendix A.5).



Theorem 2 (Complexity Analysis for PLATO).


Treating all neural network dimensions and the number of GCN layers as constants, the per-timestep cost of one PLATO training step—actor forward pass over all |Nt||N^{t}| agents and critic forward pass combined—is 𝒪​(|Nt|2+|Nt|​|Xt|)\mathcal{O}(|N^{t}|^{2}+|N^{t}||X^{t}|).

C.1 Wildfire Suppression


We simulate task openness and agent openness using the domain of wildfire suppression. The Wildfire domain [Patino et al., 2025] was developed and validated within OASYS, provides a publicly available codebase with documented configurations, and natively exhibits both AO (agents exit and re-enter as suppressant depletes) and both forms of TO (endogenous spread and exogenous random ignitions) without artificial modification, while supporting varied grid sizes for systematic generalization analysis.


Figure 2:  Wildfire example (3×33\times 3). Fires (tasks XjX_{j}) ignite, spread, burn out, or are put out (i.e., extinguished) while agents (NiN_{i}) deplete suppressant or leave for repairs. Both sets evolve over time, creating an open multi-agent system.


Each firefighter, NiN_{i}, has a suppression range, a finite suppressant level, and equipment health. Agents cannot move between cells; they act only on fires within range. When agent ii depletes its suppressant, it exits to recharge suppressant or repair its equipment and may later return, introducing agent openness.

C.2 Setup Figures


We define native (i.e., training and testing on the same grid; see Figs. 3–5) and zero-shot (i.e., training and testing on different grids; see Fig. 6). Zero-shot evaluates generalization to unseen environments, where agents must handle unseen configurations, new spatial layouts, and different coordination patterns without retraining. The same team from training is used, but on a different grid with different number of initial and possible fires and novel positions: 2×32\times 3 (3 agents, 2 fires) →\to 3×33\times 3 (3 agents, 5 fires) and 4×44\times 4 (3 agents, 7 fires); 3×33\times 3 (3 agents, 4 fires) →\to 4×44\times 4 (3 agents, 7 fires) and 5×55\times 5 (3 agents, 8 fires).


Figure 3: Setups (S0–S3) on 2×32\times 3 showing the initial suppressant level that each firefighter agent has and the fire size. Setup 1 enables fire spread (endogenous TO). Setup 2 replaces spread with random ignitions (exogenous TO) and introduces a larger fire type, testing a qualitatively different openness mechanism. Setup 3 is the most demanding: it reintroduces fire spread alongside random ignitions and adds uneven initial suppressant levels, combining both TO mechanisms with AO resource constraints. Setup 0 uses the same initial conditions as Setup 1 but disables both task openness and agent openness, yielding a static, non-open setting.


Figure 4: Setups (S0–S3) on 3×33\times 3 showing the suppressant level that each firefighter agent has and the fire size. Setup 1 enables fire spread (endogenous TO). Setup 2 replaces spread with random ignitions (exogenous TO) and introduces two larger fire types, testing a distinct openness mechanism. Setup 3 reintroduces fire spread alongside random ignitions and adds uneven initial suppressant levels, combining both TO mechanisms with AO resource constraints.


Figure 5: Setups (S0–S3) on 4×44\times 4 showing the suppressant level that each firefighter agent has and the fire size. Setup 1 enables fire spread (endogenous TO). Setup 2 replaces spread with random ignitions (exogenous TO) and introduces two larger fire types, testing a distinct openness mechanism. Setup 3 reintroduces fire spread alongside random ignitions and adds uneven initial suppressant across all six agents, combining both TO mechanisms with more heterogeneous AO.




C.2.1 Zero-Shot Evaluation


Figure 6: Example zero-shot evaluation. Agents are trained on a 2×32\times 3 Setup 0 environment and tested without retraining on a larger 3×33\times 3 Setup 0 environment.
